screens.title: Rigidbodies & Colliders — The Physics Foundation
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's physics system gives objects weight, shape, and the rules for how they push and stop each other. In this chapter you'll learn what a Rigidbody does, how Colliders define interactive shape, and why choosing the right collider matters for performance and gameplay. We'll use concrete examples — a falling crate, a static floor, and a pressure plate — to show how mass, drag, and the Is Trigger setting change behavior. You'll also learn best practices like using primitive colliders instead of expensive mesh colliders, keeping a single Rigidbody per logical object, and moving physics objects with the Rigidbody A P I rather than by changing transform directly. By the end you will be able to set up dynamic objects that respond consistently across different frame rates and avoid common mistakes that cause jitter or missed collisions. As you explore, notice how small property changes produce large differences in feel; that sensitivity is what makes physics a powerful but delicate tool. Ready to see the pieces and how they fit together?

screens.narratorSegment: Over these next screens you'll work toward practical physics skills. First, you'll be able to explain what a Rigidbody does and why it is required for objects that should fall, rotate, or be pushed. Knowing that distinction helps prevent a common mistake: adding only a Collider and expecting physical responses. Second, you'll learn to select and combine Collider types. Picking Box, Sphere, or Capsule colliders for most objects gives better performance than a full mesh. Third, you'll configure Rigidbody properties like mass, drag, angular drag, and Use Gravity to tune how objects move. A small mass or high drag changes responsiveness dramatically, so these settings are essential for gameplay feel. Finally on this screen you'll practice using the Rigidbody A P I to move objects so that the physics engine keeps control and collisions remain reliable. screens.title: What is a Rigidbody?
screens.narratorSegment: A Rigidbody is the component that gives a GameObject mass, momentum, and the ability to be moved by forces and gravity. In practical terms, adding a Rigidbody makes the object part of Unity’s physics simulation so it will fall, rotate, and respond to collisions. For example, a crate that should tumble off a ledge needs a Rigidbody; without it, the crate will simply ignore forces and remain static. The Rigidbody exposes properties such as Mass, Drag, Angular Drag, Use Gravity, and Constraints that control how the object accelerates and resists motion. Mass alters inertia: heavier objects require bigger forces to change velocity. Drag simulates air resistance to slow linear motion, while angular drag slows rotation. Use Gravity toggles whether gravity is applied automatically. Constraints let you freeze specific position or rotation axes to prevent unwanted movement, such as a character tipping over. A common misconception is that attaching a Rigidbody alone is enough to see collisions; a collider is also required for physical contact. Finally, remember to apply forces and movement through Rigidbody methods like AddForce or MovePosition so the physics engine remains authoritative. How would you tune mass and drag to make a heavy block feel different from a feather?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Rigidbody makes an object participate in physics, exposing mass, drag, gravity, and constraints to control motion.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is a Rigidbody?
Rigidbody explained

A Rigidbody makes the object subject to physics: gravity, forces, and collisions. It exposes properties to tune weight and resistance.

Mass: how much inertia the object has
Drag: linear resistance to slow movement
Angular Drag: slows rotation
Use Gravity: apply gravity automatically
Constraints: freeze axes to prevent unwanted motion
Key Takeaway

Use Rigidbody when an object should move by physics. Tune properties to shape feel and behavior.

Concrete example

A crate with Rigidbody, mass 10, and low drag will fall and resist acceleration more than one with mass 0.1. You apply push with AddForce so the engine calculates collisions and momentum correctly.

// Conceptual pseudocode (for reading)
// Attach a Rigidbody to allow physics-driven motion
GameObject crate = new GameObject("Crate");
crate.AddComponent<Rigidbody>();
crate.transform.position = new Vector3(0, 5, 0);

// Later, apply a shove using the Rigidbody API
Rigidbody rb = crate.GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
rb.AddForce(Vector3.forward * 5f, ForceMode.Impulse);
Common mistake
Moving a Rigidbody by changing transform.position bypasses physics and causes missed collisions and jitter. Use Rigidbody.MovePosition or AddForce instead.

screens.title: Configuring Rigidbody Properties
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Rigidbody properties is how you craft the physical feel of an object. Mass controls inertia: a heavy object resists acceleration and requires more force to reach the same speed as a light object. Drag simulates linear resistance; higher drag slows translational motion more quickly and can make objects feel damped or sluggish. Angular drag performs the same role for rotational motion, so high angular drag makes spinning objects settle faster. Use Gravity toggles whether gravity is applied automatically; turning it off is useful for floating platforms or custom gravity scripts. Constraints let you freeze position or rotation axes to prevent unwanted movement—common practice is to freeze rotation axes on a player character to avoid tipping over. When tuning these values, change one property at a time and observe: increasing mass while keeping the same applied force reduces acceleration, while increasing drag reduces top speed and lengthens stopping distance. A practical pitfall is using extreme values for mass and then moving the object with transform updates; the engine’s solver expects forces that match mass values. A good closing question: given a feather and a bowling ball, which settings for mass and drag produce believable differences, and why?

keyIdea.title: Tuning physics
keyIdea.text: Adjust mass and drag to shape acceleration and damping; use constraints to lock unwanted axes and Use Gravity to opt into gravity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Configuring Rigidbody Properties
Tune these properties step by step
  1. Mass: increases inertia; heavy objects accelerate slower for the same force.
  2. Drag: linear damping; raises drag to simulate air resistance.
  3. Angular Drag: rotational damping; reduces how long spin persists.
  4. Use Gravity: toggle automatic gravity application.
  5. Constraints: freeze axes to prevent undesired shifts or tipping.
Pro tip

Change one value at a time and test in Play mode. Observe acceleration and stopping distance to reason about settings.

Example scenarios
Feather
Mass: low; Drag: high. Result: slow acceleration and quick damping of motion.
Bowling ball
Mass: high; Drag: low. Result: resists acceleration and keeps momentum when pushed.
Key Takeaway

Mass and drag together determine how an object accelerates and slows; constraints keep physics stable by preventing unwanted axes of motion.

screens.title: Collider Types & When to Use Them
screens.narratorSegment: Colliders are the invisible shapes Unity uses to detect contact. Primitive colliders — Box, Sphere, and Capsule — are efficient and fast because the physics engine can compute their intersections quickly. Use Box Colliders for rectangular or box-like objects, Sphere Colliders for balls or round objects, and Capsule Colliders for characters because their shape suits a human-like standing figure. Mesh Colliders use an object's visual mesh for collisions and can represent complex geometry exactly, but they are expensive to compute. If you must use a Mesh Collider, prefer marking it as Convex when possible to simplify calculations. A common performance strategy is to approximate complex visuals with combinations of primitive colliders attached to children or the same GameObject; a car, for example, can be approximated by multiple Boxes rather than a full mesh. Another misconception is to assume a Mesh Collider is always more accurate and thus always better; in practice it costs C P U and often provides little gameplay benefit. When accuracy matters for static scenery, a Mesh Collider is fine; for many moving objects, primitives win. Consider using Is Trigger when you need overlap detection instead of physical blocking. How would you break a complex object into primitives for collision?

keyIdea.title: Collider choice
keyIdea.text: Choose primitives for performance; use mesh colliders sparingly and prefer convex meshes for moving objects.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Collider Types
Quick comparison
Box Collider
Best for rectangular shapes. Very fast and commonly used for platforms, crates, and walls.
Sphere Collider
Best for round objects and simple overlap checks. Efficient for rolling objects.
Capsule Collider
Often used for characters because it fits an upright body and slides smoothly over edges.
Mesh Colliders and performance

Mesh Colliders use visual geometry for collisions. They can be non-convex and exact, but are more expensive. When a moving object needs collision, try a convex mesh or approximate with several primitives to reduce cost.

When to use Mesh: static scenery or when exact shape is essential
When to avoid: moving objects, many dynamic objects, or high-framerate needs
Example
A car can use multiple Box Colliders for body and separate colliders for wheels rather than one expensive mesh collider.

screens.title: Triggers vs Physical Collisions
screens.narratorSegment: The Is Trigger property changes how a collider behaves: when enabled, the collider detects overlaps instead of acting as a solid barrier. This is useful for areas that should detect presence, like pickups, checkpoints, or pressure plates, without blocking movement. In contrast, a normal collider blocks objects and produces physical responses such as bouncing or stopping. A practical scenario from the chapter is a pressure plate: the plate has a Box Collider and is static (no Rigidbody); the heavy block has a Rigidbody and Box Collider. If the pressure plate's collider is set to Is Trigger, the block can overlap and the plate fires an event without being physically pushed down. Triggers call overlap events for scripting while physical collisions call collision events that the physics engine resolves. A common misconception is to use Is Trigger for safety when you actually need a blocking surface — that can let objects pass through unintentionally. When you need both detection and blocking, combine a trigger volume for detection with a separate static collider for the physical barrier, or design logic that uses contacts and triggers appropriately. Consider: when would you want a trigger instead of a collider on a moving platform?

keyIdea.title: Trigger insight
keyIdea.text: Is Trigger turns collision into overlap detection for events without blocking physical movement.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Triggers vs Collisions
Is Trigger

When enabled, collider detects overlaps and raises events but does not physically block or bounce other objects.

Use case
Area pickups, checkpoint zones, pressure plate detection without physical movement of the plate.
Event type
Triggers call overlap events for scripting, while collisions call physics collision events and create physical responses.
Concrete example

Place a heavy block with Rigidbody on a pressure plate. If the plate's collider is Is Trigger, the block overlaps and you can open a door in script without the plate moving physically.

Key Takeaway

Use Is Trigger when you need detection without physics responses. Use physical colliders when objects must stop, bounce, or block each other.

screens.title: Rigidbody + Collider Relationships
screens.narratorSegment: A key structural rule is to keep a single Rigidbody on the parent of a logical physical object and attach multiple Colliders as needed on child parts. This creates a compound collider where each child defines part of the physical boundary while the Rigidbody controls motion for the whole assembly. For example, a car can have a Rigidbody on the root GameObject and several Box Colliders on child GameObjects approximating body panels and bumpers. Adding separate Rigidbodies to each child can produce complex, hard-to-control behavior because each Rigidbody will be solved independently and interactions between them can cause jitter or unexpected rotations. Another benefit of the parent Rigidbody pattern is easier scripting: apply forces to the root Rigidbody and the whole object responds. If a child needs to act independently as a separate physical entity, then it should have its own Rigidbody, but treat that as a distinct object rather than a child of a single logical object. A common misconception is thinking that more Rigidbodies makes collisions more precise. In practice, compound colliders with a single Rigidbody usually yield simpler, more predictable physics.

keyIdea.title: Hierarchy rule
keyIdea.text: Attach one Rigidbody to a logical object and multiple colliders to compose its collision shape; avoid multiple Rigidbodies on parts of the same object.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Rigidbody & Collider Relationships
Best practice

Use one Rigidbody on the parent and multiple colliders on children to form a compound collider. Apply forces to the parent Rigidbody for predictable behavior.

Parent Rigidbody holds mass and motion.
Children hold colliders that shape contact areas.
Avoid multiple Rigidbodies on parts of the same logical object.
Example: Car body

Root GameObject: Rigidbody. Children: Box Colliders for hood, roof, and trunk. This is easier to manage than a single complex mesh collider or multiple Rigidbodies on each part.

Common mistake
Giving each visual child its own Rigidbody causes independent physical simulation and unpredictable joint effects. Prefer compound colliders unless parts truly need separate physics.
Key Takeaway

One Rigidbody per logical object plus child colliders gives stable, predictable physics behavior and simpler scripting.

screens.title: Moving Rigidbodies Correctly in Script
screens.narratorSegment: When an object has a Rigidbody, the physics engine must be the source of truth for motion. Directly assigning transform. position or transform. rotation moves the object but bypasses the physics solver, which can cause missed collisions, jitter, and inconsistent results across frame rates. Instead, use Rigidbody. MovePosition in FixedUpdate for kinematic-like movement that still interacts properly, or Rigidbody. AddForce to apply forces in a physically consistent way. For example, to push a crate forward as an impulse, call AddForce with ForceMode. Impulse in Start or in response to an input; for controlled movement you can call MovePosition inside FixedUpdate with interpolated positions. The chapter includes starter code that applies an initial AddForce to illustrate the effect. A common misconception is thinking transform updates are fine if you only move small distances; in practice the solver needs to know about movement to resolve collisions reliably. Always cache and use the Rigidbody reference, and perform physics moves in FixedUpdate so the simulation and your code operate on the same fixed timestep. Which method fits your gameplay: instantaneous shove, or smooth, controlled repositioning?

keyIdea.title: Movement rule
keyIdea.text: Use Rigidbody APIs in FixedUpdate for consistent physics; avoid direct transform changes for physics objects.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Moving Rigidbodies in Script
Starter code example
using UnityEngine;

public class ApplyInitialForce : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float forceMagnitude = 10f;
  public Vector3 forceDirection = Vector3.forward; // Pushes forward along Z-axis

  private Rigidbody rb;

  void Start()
  {
    rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
    if (rb == null)
    {
      Debug.LogError("Rigidbody not found on this GameObject!");
      return;
    }

    // Apply an initial force to the Rigidbody
    rb.AddForce(forceDirection.normalized * forceMagnitude, ForceMode.Impulse);
  }
}
This script demonstrates AddForce as an impulse. Use AddForce for force-driven motion and MovePosition for controlled repositioning in FixedUpdate.
MovePosition pattern
void FixedUpdate()
{
  Vector3 target = transform.position + inputDirection * speed * Time.fixedDeltaTime;
  rb.MovePosition(target);
}
Common mistake
Calling transform.position = ... on a Rigidbody bypasses collisions and often causes teleport-like artifacts. Use Rigidbody methods instead.

screens.title: Static Colliders and Dynamic Objects
screens.narratorSegment: Static colliders are colliders without a Rigidbody. They function as immovable objects in the physics world: walls, floors, and static scenery are typical examples. When a Rigidbody collides with a static collider, the physics engine calculates contact response and stops or bounces the Rigidbody based on its properties. Because static colliders do not move under physics, they are computationally cheaper than dynamic colliders and are preferred for environment geometry. One important detail is that colliders alone do not create physics motion — the colliding object must have a Rigidbody to react. If you accidentally remove a Rigidbody from a moving object, it will no longer be driven by physics and may pass through static colliders if repositioned via transform. A practical pattern is to keep large environment pieces as static colliders and use Rigidbodies only on objects that should move or be pushed. For a pressure plate scenario, make the ground a static collider and the block a Rigidbody-driven object so the block rests and triggers events without the floor moving. Static Colliders and Dynamic Objects means static colliders are immovable and efficient; dynamic motion requires a rigidbody on the moving object.. In practical terms, how static colliders interact with rigidbodies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Physics Problems
screens.narratorSegment: Physics bugs often come from a small set of repeatable mistakes. First, moving a physics object by setting transform. position bypasses the physics solver and often causes jitter or missed collisions; fix this by using Rigidbody. MovePosition or AddForce inside FixedUpdate. Second, forgetting to add a Collider to either party in a collision leads to no contact detection: ensure moving objects have both Rigidbody and Collider while static surfaces have only a Collider. Third, using many Mesh Colliders for moving objects can produce poor performance; replace them with primitive colliders or convex mesh colliders where possible. Fourth, attaching multiple Rigidbodies to parts of the same logical object leads to complex and hard-to-debug interactions; instead attach one Rigidbody to the parent and use child colliders. Finally, extreme values for mass or inconsistent time steps can produce unstable simulations; use reasonable ranges and test at different frame rates. For each problem, the fix is to restore physics authority to the engine and simplify collider geometry. Try to reproduce one of these issues intentionally, then apply the fixes to see how stability improves.

Common mistakes
  • Using transform.position on a Rigidbody.
  • Missing Collider on one of the objects.
  • Using complex Mesh Colliders for moving objects.
  • Multiple Rigidbodies on parts of the same object.
Fixes & tests
  1. Use Rigidbody.MovePosition or AddForce in FixedUpdate.
  2. Ensure both colliders exist and Is Trigger is set deliberately.
  3. Replace mesh colliders with primitives or convex meshes.
  4. Attach one Rigidbody to the parent and colliders to children.
Key Takeaway

Reclaim physics authority for movement and simplify collider geometry to avoid unstable behavior and performance issues.

screens.title: Short Assessment & Scenario
screens.narratorSegment: Let's apply what you've learned with a short scenario-based assessment. Imagine you are building a puzzle where the player pushes crates onto a pressure plate to open a door. Which configuration ensures the floor blocks movement while crates can be pushed? The correct design is: Floor uses a Box Collider with Is Trigger disabled and no Rigidbody, acting as a static collider; Crates use a Rigidbody and Box Collider with Is Trigger disabled so they collide and rest on the floor. Why is this correct? The static floor is efficient and immovable, while the crate's Rigidbody allows it to be affected by forces and respond to collisions. A wrong choice would be making the floor a Rigidbody or setting Is Trigger to true on the floor, which either makes the floor move or prevents it from blocking. In a second question, how would you move a crate programmatically while preserving collisions? Use Rigidbody. AddForce for impulse or Rigidbody. MovePosition inside FixedUpdate for kinematic movement. These answers test whether you understand both component selection and scripting practices needed for consistent physics behavior.

fullNarratorScript:
Unity's physics system gives objects weight, shape, and the rules for how they push and stop each other. In this chapter you'll learn what a Rigidbody does, how Colliders define interactive shape, and why choosing the right collider matters for performance and gameplay. We'll use concrete examples — a falling crate, a static floor, and a pressure plate — to show how mass, drag, and the Is Trigger setting change behavior. You'll also learn best practices like using primitive colliders instead of expensive mesh colliders, keeping a single Rigidbody per logical object, and moving physics objects with the Rigidbody A P I rather than by changing transform directly. By the end you will be able to set up dynamic objects that respond consistently across different frame rates and avoid common mistakes that cause jitter or missed collisions. As you explore, notice how small property changes produce large differences in feel; that sensitivity is what makes physics a powerful but delicate tool. Ready to see the pieces and how they fit together?

Over these next screens you'll work toward practical physics skills. First, you'll be able to explain what a Rigidbody does and why it is required for objects that should fall, rotate, or be pushed. Knowing that distinction helps prevent a common mistake: adding only a Collider and expecting physical responses. Second, you'll learn to select and combine Collider types. Picking Box, Sphere, or Capsule colliders for most objects gives better performance than a full mesh. Third, you'll configure Rigidbody properties like mass, drag, angular drag, and Use Gravity to tune how objects move. A small mass or high drag changes responsiveness dramatically, so these settings are essential for gameplay feel. Finally on this screen you'll practice using the Rigidbody A P I to move objects so that the physics engine keeps control and collisions remain reliable. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a verified competency milestone to mark practical mastery.

These additional practice goals focus on implementation and debugging. You will set up a simple scene with a FallingBlock and GroundPlatform and observe how a Box Collider with and without a Rigidbody behaves. You will change mass and drag to see how those properties alter acceleration and stopping distance. Next you'll experiment with Is Trigger to see how trigger colliders detect overlap without blocking movement, which is useful for pickups or activation zones. Finally, you will learn to identify and fix two common mistakes: moving a Rigidbody by changing transform directly, and attaching multiple independent Rigidbodies to child parts of a single logical object. Each practice goal maps to a short assessment: set properties, run the simulation, and answer why an observed behavior occurred. Achieving these will show you can configure and reason about basic physics interactions in a Unity scene.

A Rigidbody is the component that gives a GameObject mass, momentum, and the ability to be moved by forces and gravity. In practical terms, adding a Rigidbody makes the object part of Unity’s physics simulation so it will fall, rotate, and respond to collisions. For example, a crate that should tumble off a ledge needs a Rigidbody; without it, the crate will simply ignore forces and remain static. The Rigidbody exposes properties such as Mass, Drag, Angular Drag, Use Gravity, and Constraints that control how the object accelerates and resists motion. Mass alters inertia: heavier objects require bigger forces to change velocity. Drag simulates air resistance to slow linear motion, while angular drag slows rotation. Use Gravity toggles whether gravity is applied automatically. Constraints let you freeze specific position or rotation axes to prevent unwanted movement, such as a character tipping over. A common misconception is that attaching a Rigidbody alone is enough to see collisions; a collider is also required for physical contact. Finally, remember to apply forces and movement through Rigidbody methods like AddForce or MovePosition so the physics engine remains authoritative. How would you tune mass and drag to make a heavy block feel different from a feather?

Configuring Rigidbody properties is how you craft the physical feel of an object. Mass controls inertia: a heavy object resists acceleration and requires more force to reach the same speed as a light object. Drag simulates linear resistance; higher drag slows translational motion more quickly and can make objects feel damped or sluggish. Angular drag performs the same role for rotational motion, so high angular drag makes spinning objects settle faster. Use Gravity toggles whether gravity is applied automatically; turning it off is useful for floating platforms or custom gravity scripts. Constraints let you freeze position or rotation axes to prevent unwanted movement—common practice is to freeze rotation axes on a player character to avoid tipping over. When tuning these values, change one property at a time and observe: increasing mass while keeping the same applied force reduces acceleration, while increasing drag reduces top speed and lengthens stopping distance. A practical pitfall is using extreme values for mass and then moving the object with transform updates; the engine’s solver expects forces that match mass values. A good closing question: given a feather and a bowling ball, which settings for mass and drag produce believable differences, and why?

Colliders are the invisible shapes Unity uses to detect contact. Primitive colliders — Box, Sphere, and Capsule — are efficient and fast because the physics engine can compute their intersections quickly. Use Box Colliders for rectangular or box-like objects, Sphere Colliders for balls or round objects, and Capsule Colliders for characters because their shape suits a human-like standing figure. Mesh Colliders use an object's visual mesh for collisions and can represent complex geometry exactly, but they are expensive to compute. If you must use a Mesh Collider, prefer marking it as Convex when possible to simplify calculations. A common performance strategy is to approximate complex visuals with combinations of primitive colliders attached to children or the same GameObject; a car, for example, can be approximated by multiple Boxes rather than a full mesh. Another misconception is to assume a Mesh Collider is always more accurate and thus always better; in practice it costs C P U and often provides little gameplay benefit. When accuracy matters for static scenery, a Mesh Collider is fine; for many moving objects, primitives win. Consider using Is Trigger when you need overlap detection instead of physical blocking. How would you break a complex object into primitives for collision?

The Is Trigger property changes how a collider behaves: when enabled, the collider detects overlaps instead of acting as a solid barrier. This is useful for areas that should detect presence, like pickups, checkpoints, or pressure plates, without blocking movement. In contrast, a normal collider blocks objects and produces physical responses such as bouncing or stopping. A practical scenario from the chapter is a pressure plate: the plate has a Box Collider and is static (no Rigidbody); the heavy block has a Rigidbody and Box Collider. If the pressure plate's collider is set to Is Trigger, the block can overlap and the plate fires an event without being physically pushed down. Triggers call overlap events for scripting while physical collisions call collision events that the physics engine resolves. A common misconception is to use Is Trigger for safety when you actually need a blocking surface — that can let objects pass through unintentionally. When you need both detection and blocking, combine a trigger volume for detection with a separate static collider for the physical barrier, or design logic that uses contacts and triggers appropriately. Consider: when would you want a trigger instead of a collider on a moving platform?

A key structural rule is to keep a single Rigidbody on the parent of a logical physical object and attach multiple Colliders as needed on child parts. This creates a compound collider where each child defines part of the physical boundary while the Rigidbody controls motion for the whole assembly. For example, a car can have a Rigidbody on the root GameObject and several Box Colliders on child GameObjects approximating body panels and bumpers. Adding separate Rigidbodies to each child can produce complex, hard-to-control behavior because each Rigidbody will be solved independently and interactions between them can cause jitter or unexpected rotations. Another benefit of the parent Rigidbody pattern is easier scripting: apply forces to the root Rigidbody and the whole object responds. If a child needs to act independently as a separate physical entity, then it should have its own Rigidbody, but treat that as a distinct object rather than a child of a single logical object. A common misconception is thinking that more Rigidbodies makes collisions more precise. In practice, compound colliders with a single Rigidbody usually yield simpler, more predictable physics.

When an object has a Rigidbody, the physics engine must be the source of truth for motion. Directly assigning transform. position or transform. rotation moves the object but bypasses the physics solver, which can cause missed collisions, jitter, and inconsistent results across frame rates. Instead, use Rigidbody. MovePosition in FixedUpdate for kinematic-like movement that still interacts properly, or Rigidbody. AddForce to apply forces in a physically consistent way. For example, to push a crate forward as an impulse, call AddForce with ForceMode. Impulse in Start or in response to an input; for controlled movement you can call MovePosition inside FixedUpdate with interpolated positions. The chapter includes starter code that applies an initial AddForce to illustrate the effect. A common misconception is thinking transform updates are fine if you only move small distances; in practice the solver needs to know about movement to resolve collisions reliably. Always cache and use the Rigidbody reference, and perform physics moves in FixedUpdate so the simulation and your code operate on the same fixed timestep. Which method fits your gameplay: instantaneous shove, or smooth, controlled repositioning?

Static colliders are colliders without a Rigidbody. They function as immovable objects in the physics world: walls, floors, and static scenery are typical examples. When a Rigidbody collides with a static collider, the physics engine calculates contact response and stops or bounces the Rigidbody based on its properties. Because static colliders do not move under physics, they are computationally cheaper than dynamic colliders and are preferred for environment geometry. One important detail is that colliders alone do not create physics motion — the colliding object must have a Rigidbody to react. If you accidentally remove a Rigidbody from a moving object, it will no longer be driven by physics and may pass through static colliders if repositioned via transform. A practical pattern is to keep large environment pieces as static colliders and use Rigidbodies only on objects that should move or be pushed. For a pressure plate scenario, make the ground a static collider and the block a Rigidbody-driven object so the block rests and triggers events without the floor moving.
